title: Electrical Systems
seo_title: Secondary 2 Science: Electrical Systems Worksheets (Lower Secondary Science with Answers)
standard_text: Describe current, potential difference and resistance and their SI units; draw and interpret circuit diagrams with cells, switches, lamps, fixed and variable resistors, ammeters and voltmeters; investigate current in series and parallel circuits; describe applications of the chemical, heating and magnetic effects of current; state electrical hazards and safety precautions; explain power and calculate the cost of electricity using kWh (summary of the MOE Lower Secondary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 2 science worksheets for Singapore students on electricity: current, voltage, resistance, series and parallel circuits, effects of current, safety and the cost of electricity. With answers.
key_big: Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.
body_html:
How to think about it

Current flows when a potential difference pushes charge round a complete circuit.

  • Current: amperes (A), measured by an ammeter in series. Potential difference: volts (V), measured by a voltmeter in parallel. Resistance: ohms (Ω).
  • More resistance means less current. A variable resistor changes the current.
  • Effects of current: heating (kettle, fuse), magnetic (motor, bell), chemical (electroplating, charging).
  • Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (h). Cost = kWh × price per kWh. Use fuses and earthing to stay safe.
Example

A 1.5 kW air-conditioner runs for 4 h at 30 cents per kWh. Cost?

1.5 × 4 = 6 kWh

6 × 30

Answer: 180 cents ($1.80)

Example

How is an ammeter connected?

Current must pass through it

Answer: in series

Common mistakes

  • Saying current is used up by a lamp. The current is the same all round a series circuit.
  • Connecting an ammeter in parallel or a voltmeter in series.
  • Calling kWh a unit of power. It is a unit of energy.
  • Thinking a bigger fuse is always safer. It must suit the appliance.

faq.a: Multiply power in kW by time in hours to get kWh, then multiply by the price per kWh.
